items.caseName: State of U.P. & Ors. v. Grand Slam Fitness (P) Ltd.
items.coram: Justice S.V.N. Bhatti and Justice Shree Chandrashekhar
items.headline: Treadmills, exercise bikes and gym equipment are 'sports goods' exempt from UP VAT
items.text: The Supreme Court dismissed Uttar Pradesh's appeals and upheld the High Court's order setting aside the tax demands. Comparing the sports-goods entry in the commodity code with the 9 April 2008 exemption notification, it held that fitness equipment such as treadmills, exercise bikes, rowers and strength machines counts as sports goods. The Revenue therefore could not tax them at 12.5% as unclassified goods under the UP VAT Act, 2008.
items.why: Settles a long-running classification dispute for fitness equipment sellers under the old VAT regime.

items.caseName: Hemant Ankush Balwadkar v. State of Maharashtra and Anr.
items.headline: Denying extra firearms to an eligible sport shooter curbs his right to take part in sport
items.text: The High Court held that refusing a shooter permission to acquire additional arms, though he was eligible under a Central Government notification, infringed his fundamental right to pursue his chosen sport. A pending criminal case in which he had no assigned role and no violence was alleged could not justify action under Section 17 of the Arms Act. The Police Commissioner's and State's orders were quashed and six additional arms were directed to be endorsed on his licence within seven days.

items.caseName: Amrit Wilson v. Union of India & Ors.
items.headline: Centre's order cancelling author Amrit Wilson's OCI card gave no details of alleged 'anti-India activities'
items.text: The High Court found that the show cause notice and the order cancelling the UK-based author's OCI card did not say what the alleged anti-India activities were, so she had no fair chance to reply. It told the authorities to issue a fresh notice within a week with specific reasons, giving a redacted gist or inspection of material if full disclosure is not possible. The cancellation stays in force for four weeks or until a fresh order is passed, whichever comes first.
items.why: Reinforces that natural justice applies to OCI cancellations even when national security is cited.

items.caseName: Subhash Chander Malhotra v. Raman Malhotra & Ors.
items.headline: Senior citizen can't be made to share his own house with children against his wishes
items.text: The High Court allowed an 85-year-old man's petition and ordered his eldest son and daughter-in-law to vacate his self-acquired Delhi property within four weeks. It held that a senior citizen seeking eviction of children under the Senior Citizens Act need not prove ill-treatment; showing that the property needs protection so he can live there in peace is enough. The District Magistrate's and Divisional Commissioner's orders were set aside, and the local SHO was told to help enforce the order.
items.why: Lowers the evidential bar for elderly owners seeking summary eviction of children.

items.caseName: Namrata Yadav v. Ramesh Kumar Yadav & Ors.
items.headline: Daughter-in-law can't be asked to leave senior in-laws' house without assured alternate accommodation
items.text: The High Court upheld the direction that a woman and her son leave her in-laws' home, but found the alternate-accommodation terms too vague to protect her right of residence. It said a three-week window was unjustified since she had lived there since 2008 and her son is in Class XII. The in-laws must pay rent of up to Rs 35,000 a month, with six months deposited in advance, once she identifies a place within four weeks, until her residence right is finally decided.

items.coram: Justice Vivek Chaudhary and Justice Renu Bhatnagar
items.headline: Fresh divorce petition maintainable even after earlier one was withdrawn for lack of jurisdiction
items.text: A Division Bench held that a husband who withdrew his divorce petition because the court lacked territorial jurisdiction, without leave to refile, is not barred from filing again in the proper court. Procedural rules should not defeat substantive matrimonial rights where the withdrawal was in good faith and the claim was never decided on merits. The wife's appeal against the Family Court's refusal to reject the second petition was dismissed, distinguishing Nidhi Jain v. Ankit Jain.

items.headline: Custody fights must put child's welfare first, not parents' 'battle of wits and egos'
items.text: Disposing of a father's contempt plea alleging the mother blocked court-ordered visitation, the High Court said it was too early to find wilful disobedience while execution proceedings and her appeal were pending. It declined to start contempt action. The Family Court was directed to take up the father's execution petition and pass substantive orders.

items.caseName: Bebika Chettri v. High Court of Sikkim
items.headline: Suspended officiating District Judge of Soreng ordered reinstated pending disciplinary proceedings
items.text: The High Court ordered the immediate reinstatement of the suspended officiating District Judge, subject to the outcome of the disciplinary inquiry. Continued suspension was unnecessary because all witnesses had been examined and only final arguments remained. The inquiry must end within a month with her cooperation, and whether to give her judicial work was left to the High Court administration.
